questions.question: Describe the old ideas about the causes of disease before Pasteur.
questions.expected_answer: People did not know germs cause disease. Many believed in the miasma theory, that diseases came from bad air or poisonous smells from rubbish, sewage and swamps, and some still believed in the four humours. Many scientists believed in spontaneous generation, that living things such as maggots or tiny creatures appear from nothing. In 1847, Semmelweis showed that doctors washing their hands saved mothers, but many doctors refused to believe him.

questions.question: Explain Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiment and what it proved.
questions.expected_answer: Pasteur put broth into flasks, bent their long necks into an S shape like a swan's neck and boiled the broth to kill germs. Air could enter, but dust and germs were trapped in the curve, so the broth stayed fresh. When he broke the neck or tipped the flask so the broth touched the trapped dust, the broth went bad. This proved spontaneous generation was wrong and that germs from the air make things go bad, supporting germ theory, the idea that germs cause disease.

questions.question: Describe Pasteur's work on vaccines and his legacy.
questions.expected_answer: Pasteur's team found that weakened chicken cholera germs protected chickens, so he used weakened germs to make vaccines and named them in honour of Jenner. In 1881, he publicly showed that vaccinated sheep survived anthrax while unvaccinated sheep died, and in 1885 he saved nine-year-old Joseph Meister from rabies. His work gave us pasteurisation, better hygiene such as hand washing, boiling water and sterilising, inspired surgeons to fight infection, and led to the Pasteur Institute in 1888.
